item.title: 'Glaciers in Himalayas retreating': Nepal floods triggered by 'glacier collapse & massive landslide'
item.description: Annette Young is pleased to welcome Joseph Shea, Glaciologist and Associate Professor at the University of Northern BC. Shea argues that the catastrophe should be understood as a compound event in which a glacier failure and a massive landslide occurred together. His analysis places the disaster within the broader, well-established transformation of the Himalayas under climate change. As warming changes high-mountain environments, scientists may increasingly need to identify subtle precursors to rare but potentially devastating cascading hazards. Fuente: France 24 - English.

item.description: Who dreams of having a Euro summer now when staying in an ancient, uncooled building in the Old Town is like trying to sleep in a wood-fired pizza oven? This week the Euro summer comes to an end – and so does a certain type of posting on Instagram. Waiting at the bus stop in the grey winter dawn, a slanting rain soaking your trouser leg, you can warm yourself by scrolling your feed and seeing pictures of Australians enjoying a Euro summer. item.title: Iceland’s close ties with EU mean no vote is not a Brexit-style rejection
item.description: A yes to membership would have given Brussels a boost but Icelanders have not voted to isolate themselves Iceland’s 52.8% to 47.2% vote against reopening EU accession talks is, undeniably, a blow for Brussels. But claiming it as a Brexit-style victory for “national sovereignty” or evidence of broad rejection of the EU misrepresents the reality of the island’s relationship with the bloc. For the EU, Iceland was a dream candidate: small, stable, prosperous and strategically located in an increasingly contested Arctic. Eager as it is to wield more geopolitical clout and revive flagging momentum… Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: IncaDivide 2026: el Everest del ultraciclismo en el Valle Sagrado de los Incas en Perú
item.description: El 29 de agosto terminó el IncaDivide de Urubamba, en Perú. Se trata de una de las carreras de ciclismo de ultradistancia más exigentes, en donde los participantes recorrieron 1.200 km por rutas en grava en nueve días sin asistencia externa y en autosuficiencia total a través de los Andes peruanos. Cada corredor debía gestionar sus horas de sueño, su comida, cuántos kilómetros recorría al día y qué equipaje llevar. El francés Pierre Rolland fue el ganador y la leyenda peruana Rodney Soncco quedó segundo. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
